src.copy: Joseph Hammer (trans.), Ancient Alphabets and Hieroglyphic Characters Explained (London: W. Bulmer and Co., 1806). Copy used: the Wellcome Library's, Internet Archive identifier b22039910 (https://archive.org/details/b22039910). Images come from the item's processed JP2s (b22039910_jp2.zip), used at full pixel size: 2093x2896 for the Arabic pages and 2241x3020 for the English, 300 ppi according to the record. Leaf numbers come from b22039910_scandata.xml, and n = leaf - 1. I checked that mapping against https://archive.org/download/b22039910/page/n<N>.jpg for all ten leaves used: the images match exactly. No other copy was needed, because none of the chosen pages has a blot or a cropped margin. In a left-to-right scan the Arabic part runs backwards, so Arabic p. p = leaf 223 - p. English text p. p = leaf p + 30.
src.rights:
The metadata.rights field of https://archive.org/metadata/b22039910, quoted exactly: This work is available under the Creative Commons, Public Domain Mark. Statement: "This work is available under the Creative Commons, Public Domain Mark". URL as given: http://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/mark/1.0/. That http URL would not resolve from this environment; the https form, https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/mark/1.0/, was fetched and answered 200. The same record also has a field that reads, verbatim, notes = "Copyright in title page
". The record does not explain it. The title page of this copy (leaf 5) and its verso (leaf 6) were read: they carry the title, the imprint (London: W. Bulmer and Co., 1806), the library’s accession number and its stamp, and no copyright statement. The printing of 1806 is in the public domain (Hammer died in 1856), as the record’s own rights field states, and the note is not read as a restriction on the plates. None of the other five copies has a rights field. The two Oxford/Google scans carry possible-copyright-status NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT.

jobs.heading: الباب الثاني في الاقلام السبعة المشهورة . الفصل الاول من الباب الثاني في القلم السرياني — Hammer: "CHAPTER II. The seven most celebrated old alphabets. SECTION I. The Syrian alphabet, (v. orig. p. 9.)" [English p. 4]
jobs.order: abjad, the 22 letters ا to ت only (rows 9+8+5); no ث خ ذ ض ظ غ
jobs.notes: Complete and clear, with an Arabic letter printed under every sign. The forms are cursive, Syriac-like letters drawn with thick and thin strokes: trace the pen's centre line. They drift from real Syriac, and the drift is the record, so do not correct them from a modern chart. I chose this over the Musnad (p. 14, 28 signs) and the old Nabataean (p. 10, 28 signs) because the site's Syriac hall can be set beside it. The book has two more Syriac tables in its last section, neither traced: p. 117 (22 signs, 'according to the ancient sages') and p. 118 (21 signs, the form 'of our time', with ع not printed).

jobs.heading: الفصل الثاني عشر من الباب الرابع في صفة قلم الحكيم هرمس ابوطاط الذي كتب الصنعة الشريفة . وصنع باقليم الصعيد كنوزا وبرابي ونواويس كاهنية له ولولده . ورصدها ورمزها بهذا القلم . الذي استخرجه من السرب المظلم — Hammer: "SECTION XII. The alphabet of Hermes Abootat the philosopher. … extracted from the regions of darkness, (v. orig. p. 34.)" [Chapter IV, English pp. 6-7]
jobs.order: abjad (rows 10+9+9: ا…ي / ك…ق / ر ش ت ث خ ذ ض ظ غ)
jobs.notes: Fine-line signs with small open rings at the ends of strokes, which the glyph kit's rings can draw. The signs are small (roughly 60-110 px tall in the crop), so trace at full resolution. I preferred this to the Hermes table on p. 16: that one is partly pictorial (a bird, a tree, a face) and has 21 signs under 22 letters, with ر and ش printed under a single sign. The book prints this table in Bāb IV, among the sages' pens. The Arabic name is هرمس ابوطاط, Abū Ṭāṭ; Hammer prints "Abootat".

jobs.heading: الفصل الرابع عشر من الباب الرابع في صفة قلم الحكيم سيوريانوس الذي الف كتب الفلك . واسرار النجوم . والطلسمات وخواصها . والرصد . وعمل خواتيم الكواكب . وتسخير روحانياتها وجلبها — Hammer: "SECTION XIV. The alphabet of Syourianos the philosopher, (v. orig. p. 36.) He wrote in this alphabet on astronomy, … on the effects of planet-rings; and on the invocation and conjuration of spirits." [Chapter IV, English p. 7]
jobs.order: abjad (rows 9+8+7+4: ا…ط / ي…ف / ص ق ر ش ت ث خ / ذ ض ظ غ)
jobs.notes: The clearest ring-letter table in the book, of the charaktêres kind. Nearly every stroke ends in an open ring, and some signs carry 5-7 rings, so count the rings at full resolution. The hardest signs are the interlaced X-forms in row 4 (ذ ض ظ غ). In row 3 the sign over ص runs close to its neighbour. The heading credits Siyūriyānūs with books on the making of the planets' seals (خواتيم الكواكب): report that as the book's claim, not as a link to the seven seals.

jobs.heading: الفصل الثالث من الباب الثالث في صفة قلم الحكيم افلاطون — Hammer: "SECTION III. The alphabet of Plato, (v. orig. p. 18.)" [Chapter III, English p. 5]
jobs.order: abjad to ت (rows 9+9+4: ا…ط / ي…ص / ق ر ش ت)
jobs.notes: The optional second table for the sages: short, clear and simply drawn (a small circle, Δ, Z, a right triangle, a bar, curls, boxes). Watch the sign for ه: it is one heavy dot standing in the row of separator dots and is told from them only by its size and by the ه printed under it. Leave it out if only one table per kind is wanted. The book has a second Plato table, 'the natural tree pen' (p. 46, 30 signs), not chosen.

jobs.heading: الفصل الثاني من الباب الخامس في صفة قلم كوكب المشتري وهيته كما تري فافهم — Hammer: "CHAPTER V. The Alphabets of the Seven Planets. … SECTION II. The alphabet of Jupiter, (v. orig. p. 48.)" [English p. 10]
jobs.order: abjad (rows 8+8+8+4: ا…ح / ط…ع / ف ص ق ر ش ت ث خ / ذ ض ظ غ)
jobs.notes: The book gives all seven planetary alphabets (Bāb V, Arabic pp. 47-53): Saturn, Jupiter, Mars ('the sage Bahrām'), the Sun, Venus ('Anāhīd'), Mercury ('who is Hermes') and the Moon. I chose Jupiter as the clearest complete table with ring-ends. Some strokes end in heavy filled blobs rather than open rings (for example ا, ف and the ظ/غ forms): draw those as dots, not rings. Alternatives: Mercury (p. 52) is just as clear but purely linear; Saturn, the Sun and the Moon are partly pictorial.

facsimileOnly: hermesian-letters, Arabic p. 120 (leaf 103, n102) — 'Hieroglyphs read as letters'. Shown as a facsimile only because the signs are pictorial (birds, vessels, a human figure, a domed building, an eye, a serpent), and pen strokes would misrepresent them. Files: plates/ibn-wahshiyya/hermesian-letters/page.jpg and crop.png, plus supplementary crops of the table's first row on p. 119 (crop-p119-first-row.png, leaf 104) and last row on p. 121 (crop-p121-last-row.png, leaf 102). The table is the Shīshīm pen 'according to the Harāmisa' (Arabic p. 119: صفة قلم شيشيم الذي تعلمه بالوحي … وهذه صفته علي راي الهرامسة). Hammer's English (pp. 43-46) is 'The characters of the Hermesians, with the particular names and powers of their letters', laid out as Character / Name / Power. The page has 26 signs (7+7+6+6), each with its printed value. I count 37 signs across pp. 119-121; the text says 38.

first-series-hieroglyphs, English p. 19 (leaf 49, n48) — 'Hieroglyphs read as signs of things and ideas'. Shown as a facsimile only because the signs are pictorial (faces, a hand, a serpent, hatched discs). Files: plates/ibn-wahshiyya/first-series-hieroglyphs/page.jpg and crop.png; the crop includes the heading 'THE FIRST SERIES. Hieroglyphics to express Words relative to Animal Actions and Affections.' It holds 25 signs, each with Hammer's English meaning printed beneath, from Life, Death, Richness … to Action, Stroke. The Arabic counterpart is supplied too: Arabic p. 85 (leaf 138; page-arabic-p85.jpg and crop-arabic-p85.png), headed المرتبة الاولي في ذكر الاسما الحيوانية واشكالها مفردا مفردا من ساير الانواع وافعالها وحركاتها, with 21 signs and Arabic meanings in the same sequence.
findings: COUNT (settles the module's 'no count'): the book prints 86 tables. 82 are letter tables: Bāb I 5 (Kufi, Maghribi, three sorts of Indian numerals, Arabic pp. 4-8); Bāb II 7 (pp. 9-15); Bāb III 7 (pp. 16-22); Bāb IV 24 (pp. 23-46); Bāb V 7 planets (pp. 47-53); Bāb VI 12 zodiac signs (pp. 54-65); Bāb VII 10 kings (pp. 68-77); and the closing section al-Khātima al-farīda (Hammer's 'Appendix') 10 (pp. 114-134). The other 4 are hieroglyph sign tables in Bāb VIII (celestial pp. 82-84, animals pp. 85-89, plants pp. 101-107, minerals pp. 108-113). Hammer's preface gives 'the eighty alphabets herein deciphered' (p. iv) and 'the four tables of hieroglyphics' (p. xii). Counting the Indian 'three different sorts' as one alphabet gives 80; Hammer does not say that is how he counted.

WHERE THE TABLES ARE: every letter table is printed in the Arabic part (pp. 1-136, paginated from the back of the volume; Hammer: 'See page 4 of the Arabic text beginning from the right', English p. 3). The English cites them as 'v. orig. p. N'. The English part reprints only the hieroglyph series (English pp. 17-40), the Hermesian letter table (pp. 43-46) and the inline sign groups (pp. 48-49). So the module's drawing.follows ('the tables printed with the Arabic text, each cited by page') is right, and citations should read 'Arabic p. N'.

PLANETARY ALPHABETS are present, all seven: Arabic p. 47 'الباب الخامس من كتاب شوق المستهام في معرفة رموز الاقلام في معرفة اقلام الكواكب السبعة من زحل الي القمر'; English p. 10 'CHAPTER V. The Alphabets of the Seven Planets.' Two headings tie a planet to a person: Mars is 'قلم الحكيم بهرام وهو قلم كوكب المريخ' (p. 49) and Mercury is 'كوكب عطارد وهو هرمس كاتب الفلك' (p. 52; Hammer: 'Mercury or Hermes, the secretary of heaven').

KINDS NOT IN THE REGISTER, confirmed on the page (the module's own comment had held them back): twelve zodiac alphabets (Arabic pp. 54-65; English p. 10 'CHAPTER VI. The Alphabets of the Twelve Constellations.'), ten kings' alphabets (pp. 68-77; English p. 12 'CHAPTER VII. Alphabets of ancient Kings, viz: the Kings of Syria, the Hermesian Kings of Egypt, the Pharaohs, the Canaanites, Curds, Casdanians, Persians and Cophts.'), and the 'three usual alphabets' (Kufi, Maghribi, Indian numerals; English p. 3). The register's scriptNote is right that its list is incomplete: these three kinds make up 27 of the 86 tables.

HERMES AMONG THE SAGES: the book's own Bāb III heading counts Hermes as one of the seven sages: 'الباب الثالث في معرفة الاقلام الحكما السبعة المشهورين وهم هرمس واقليمون وافلاطون وفيثاغورس واسقلينوس وسقراط وارسطوس' (Arabic p. 16; Hammer, English p. 4: 'CHAPTER III. The particular Alphabets (or rather Cyphers) of the seven most celebrated Philosophers. SECTION I. The alphabet of Hermes'). The register separates Hermes from the sages, which is the page's own grouping, as its scriptNote says. The Hermes tables are p. 16 (Hermes) and p. 34 (Hermes Abū Ṭāṭ, in Bāb IV); Hermes is also named on p. 52 (Mercury), p. 70 (king Kīmās al-Hirmisī), in Bāb VIII (Hermes al-Akbar) and on pp. 119-121 (the Harāmisa).

SAGES ARE NOT ALL GREEK: the module's family and links speak of 'Greek sages', but the sages' chapters include 'الحكيم زوسيم العبري' (p. 43; Hammer 'Zosimus, a Jew philosopher'), 'حكما الاقباط' (p. 41, invented by Qifṭrīm 'of the sons of Noah'), 'سبعة من حكما الروم' led by Diyūjānis (p. 42), and the Dāwūdī pen 'كثير الاستعمال ببلاد الهند' (p. 39).

TREE ALPHABETS: the term is the book's own, used twice: 'ديسقوريدوس وهو المشجر' (Arabic p. 38; Hammer, English p. 8, 'commonly called the Tree alphabet') and 'القلم المشجر الطبيعي لافلاطون الحكيم' (p. 46; Hammer's English, p. 9, does not call it a tree alphabet). Hammer's preface, p. v: 'The commonest of them is the alphabet called by the author the tree alphabet.' This settles the research file's low-confidence card on 'al-mushajjar' (two tables, stem-and-branch signs).

HIEROGLYPHS AS SIGNS, IN THE BOOK'S OWN WORDS: Arabic p. 81 'واعلم ان هذا القلم ليس كساير الاقلام مرتبا علي الحروف بل هو رموز واشارات'; English p. 16 'It does not consist in a series of letters like other alphabets, but in expressions composed according to the arrangement made by Hermes the great.' The same page gives the signs to Hermes: 'قلم الحكيم هرمس الاكبر وهو القلم المكتوب علي البرابي والهرمات والنواويس' (p. 81). This bears out the module's intro and its kind 6.

HIEROGLYPHS READ AS LETTERS — this contradicts the module's wording: the claims entry and intro para. 4 speak of 'the frame of its letter table, one sign to each Arabic letter'. The pages show something else. The letter-valued Egyptian table is the Shīshīm pen 'according to the Harāmisa', and it stands in the closing section, not in the Hermes chapter (Arabic pp. 119-121; English pp. 43-46). The book says it has 38 letters, more than Arabic has: 'فهذه جملة حروفه وعدتها ثمانية وثلاثين حرفا . لان فيها حروف لاتوجد في اللسان العربي والعجمي' (p. 121). These include پ, چ and qualified letters such as 'نون مد' and 'كاف مايلة' (p. 120). The book also says they are not in abjad order: 'بخلاف قاعدة ابجد وغيرها . بل مرتبتهم علي حسب نطق لسانهم' (p. 122); Hammer, English p. 47: 'They are arranged in a contrary order to that commonly received of A, B, C.' Unresolved: I count 37 signs on pp. 119-121 against the stated 38. Hammer's 38-row table includes 'Zayimap', whose sign I did not find on the Arabic pages. The serpent sign is labelled غ in the Arabic (p. 120) but 'Kh' in Hammer (p. 45).

NO 'ALPHABET OF THE KABBALISTS': no such heading appears among the Arabic headings or in Hammer's English contents (English pp. 3-14). The only near word is in Hammer's note on Colphotorios, 'cabalistic spells' (English p. 7). The module was right to leave it out.

TITLE AND AUTHOR AS PRINTED: 'شوق المستهام في معرفة رموز الاقلام' heads Bāb IV (p. 23), Bāb V ('من كتاب …', p. 47) and Bāb VI (p. 54). The copyist's colophon (p. 136) reads 'وهو كتاب شوق المستهام في معرفة رموز الاقلام تاليف احمد بن ابوبكر بن وحشية النبطي الكلداني'. That matches the module's title form and Hammer's title-page 'Ahmad Bin Abubekr Bin Wahshih'.

DATE OF DEPOSIT (bears on the claim that the book closes 'under a date long after that caliph's death'): Arabic p. 135 'وجعلته ذخيرة لخزانة حضرة امير المومنين عبد الملك بن مروان … يوم الخميس المبارك ثالث شهر رمضان سنة احدي واربعين ومايتين' (Thursday 3 Ramaḍān 241). Hammer's English, p. 54, has 'Tuesday, the third of the month of Ramazán, in the year two hundred and forty-one': the weekday differs. Hammer's preface, p. xix, gives 'in the year 214', which does not match the text.

COLOPHON OF THE COPIES (bears on firstAttestation.notes, 'not established', and on Hämeen-Anttila's copyist): Arabic p. 136 reads 'فرغ من كتابة النسخة المكتوبة من الاصل المذكور حسن بن فرج بن علي بن داود بن سنان بن ثابت بن قره الحراني البابلي النوقاني يوم الثلاث المبارك سابع ربيع الاخر سنة اربعماية وثلاثة عشر وقد تمت النسخة المنقولة هذه النسخة عنها يوم الاحد المبارك ثاني محرم الحرام من شهور سنة ستة وستين وماية والف ١١٦٦ وكان النجاز من نساخته يوم الجمعة المبارك عاشر شهر جمادي الاخر سنة ستة وستين وماية والف ١١٦٦ الموافق ثاني شهر نيسان من شهور مسيحية سنة ١٧٥٣'. Read as it stands: Ḥasan ibn Faraj … al-Nūqānī finished writing the copy taken from the said original on Tuesday 7 Rabīʿ II 413; the copy from which this copy was transcribed was completed (تمت) on Sunday 2 Muḥarram 1166; and this copy was finished on Friday 10 Jumādā II 1166, equated with 2 Nīsān 1753. The Arabic does not call Ḥasan's copy the first, and the 2 Muḥarram date goes with تمت, whose subject is the exemplar, not the start of this copy: the exemplar may be an intermediate copy. Hammer's English (p. 54) reads otherwise: 'The first copy of the manuscript before us, was taken from the original by Hasan Bin Faraj … Tuesday the seventh of the month of Rabi-ul-ákhir, in the year four hundred and thirteen of the Hijrah; and this copy (the one from which this was printed), which was made from it, was begun Monday the second of the month of Muharram, in the year of the Hijrah, one thousand, one hundred, and sixty-six. And it was finished on Friday, the tenth of the month of Jamádí ul Akhir, of the same year.' His English omits the Christian date. By its own colophon, Hammer's exemplar was finished in 1166 AH / 1753. Hammer's preface, p. xix, says he found it 'at Cairo amongst the Arabs'.

THE AUTHOR'S TRAVELS (bears on Hämeen-Anttila's point cited in the module): Arabic p. 115 'وقد رايت بارض الصعيد نواويسا وبرابي واحجارا مرقومة بهذا القلم'; English p. 41 'I have myself seen in Upper Egypt, inscription tables and stones engraved with this alphabet.' On Baghdad the Arabic (p. 135) says 'نحو ثلاثين كتابا' ('about thirty'), Hammer's English (p. 53) says 'thirty-three inscriptions', and his preface (p. xiv) says 'thirty-two inscriptions'.

TABLES NOT FULLY KEYED (qualifies the scriptNote's 'Every table is set against the Arabic letters'): Indian sort 1 (p. 6) labels groups of numerals, not single signs. Aristotle (p. 22) has 31 signs under 25 letters. Hermes (p. 16) has 21 signs under 22 letters. Ptolemy (p. 26) and Marqūnus (p. 27) skip ر and ز. Arkaghānis (p. 45) skips ه. The later Syriac table (p. 118) skips ع. The 'hidden pen' (p. 129) skips ي. Aquarius (p. 64) has 30 signs with an unresolved last row. The Kurdish-claimed pen (p. 134) ends with 7 unvalued signs ('وباقي هذه الحروف لم وجدنا لها نطق ولا امثال في لغة ولا قلم', p. 135). The author's preface also says the values were 'written underneath with red ink'; Hammer's footnote: 'This distinction, for obvious reasons, has not been imitated in the printed copy.'

MISPRINTS IN HAMMER'S ENGLISH, so cite the Arabic page: Gemini is '(v. orig. p. 66.)', but the table is on p. 56 (English p. 11). Davidian is '(v. orig. p. 38.)', but the table is on p. 39 (English p. 8). The minerals series is headed 'THE FOURTH SERIES' (English p. 36), while English p. 35 calls it 'the Third Series' and the Arabic 'المرتبة الثالثة' (p. 107). The antediluvian alphabet is named three ways: 'Mimshim' (preface p. viii), 'Shíshím' (p. 41) and 'Shímshím' (p. 43); the Arabic has 'شيشيم' (pp. 114, 119).

NAMES AS PRINTED vs HAMMER: اقليمون → 'Cleomenes' (p. 17); اسقليبوس, spelled اسقلينوس in the list on p. 16 → 'Scalinus' (p. 20); ارسطوس → 'Aristotle' (p. 22); هرمس ابوطاط → 'Hermes Abootat' (p. 34); سيوريانوس → 'Syourianos' (p. 36); ذيمقراطيس → 'Democrates' (p. 40); the king's name on p. 75 is printed as صا followed by repeated alifs → 'Saaa'. Use the Arabic forms with Hammer's in brackets, never his guesses as identifications.

Final state: glyphkit/check.mjs reports ok for all three tables (22, 28 and 28 letters, 0 gaps). The overlays of trace on print and the specimen sheets were made again from the corrected files and read. Confidence counts: Syriac 22 high. Hermes 26 high and 2 medium (#8 ḥāʾ, #13 mīm). Siyuryanus 18 high, 9 medium and 1 low (#24 khāʾ); the tables field has no slot for 'low', so that one sign is reported here.

Labels and order: I read every printed Arabic letter beside its sign on all three plates; all 78 agree with the abjad order and row counts in glyphs.json. Syriac: rows 9/8/5, ا to ت. Hermes: rows 10/9/9, ا to غ. Siyuryanus: rows 9/8/7/4, ا to غ. No mislabelled or misordered sign was found.

Cells: I re-cut the cells from the JP2 master (b22039910_0214.jp2) at the recorded master_xywh with 2.25x Lanczos, and they match the stored cells pixel for pixel (max difference 0). All cells in a table share one 200 px scale, as claimed.

Other copies: I fetched two more copies of the 1806 printing. Getty Research Institute (ancientalphabets01ibnw): page images n215, n190, n188. University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill (ancientalphabets00ibnw): page images n14, n39, n41. Both metadata records say 1806 and have no rights field. Each page was registered onto the Wellcome master (SIFT similarity, 137-400 inliers, scale 1.21-1.26) and cut into the same cells. Every sign was compared in all three copies. The downloaded pages and the registered cells were working files and are not kept. Every URL recorded in glyphs.json urlsFetched answered 200 when I fetched it.

Where the copies differ: (a) Syriac tāʾ: the faint tick above it is in the Wellcome scan only. (b) Hermes thāʾ: the fork at the left end of the bar is a blot in Wellcome, heavy in Getty and a clear two-pronged fork in UNC. (c) Siyuryanus ḍād: the upper-right curl is open in Wellcome and Getty but closed in UNC, and the eye between the lower-left ring and the stem appears only in Wellcome. (d) Siyuryanus jīm: the two strokes run together in Wellcome but are separated by a hairline in Getty and UNC. (e) Syriac jīm: the space between the upper prongs is open in Wellcome and Getty and closed in UNC. All other signs have the same form in all three copies.

Measuring method: the checker measured (1) how much of the traced centre line lies off the ink, (2) how much of the ink skeleton the trace covers, (3) distance and offset between trace and skeleton for each subpath, (4) enclosed counters, comparing what the kit pen draws with the holes in each copy, and (5) straight-line fits to the skeleton in all three copies. After the corrections no subpath is off the ink. The remaining median offsets of 1.1-1.6 units (Hermes 14, 19, 24, 27; Siyuryanus 10, 16, 18, 27, 28) stay inside the printed stroke and were left alone.

Limits of the kit pen that remain, all stated in notes or conventions: the small triangular heads of Siyuryanus kāf, shīn and thāʾ have openings only a speck wide in all copies, and these fill in at pen 5.5, so the heads read as solid. The opening of the Hermes ṣād pennant is smaller than printed. The triangle of Siyuryanus bāʾ is drawn about 1.3 times its printed size so that its clearly printed opening stays open. The inner stroke in the top loop of Siyuryanus khāʾ is not drawn, which is why that sign is now low.
corrections: Syriac #2 bāʾ: the base's left upright was drawn about 2.5 units left of the print. Moved from (28,45.5)-(25.5,56.5) to (30.8,45)-(27.4,56), matching the UNC skeleton fit; the start of the base was adjusted to match.

Syriac #3 jīm: in all three copies the long lower counter is closed where the two sides pinch, but the drawing left a 7-unit gap there, so the counter was open at the pen width. Added a short join, M 46.3 41.5 L 41 48. The note now records the pinch and that the upper prongs are closed in UNC.

Syriac #6 wāw: the ring was drawn too small and too high; its bottom was at y 59 against about 62 in the print. Redrawn from the heavy square end at the upper left, over the top, down, round and up the left, stopping short of the start. The strokes text was rewritten to match.

Syriac #17 fāʾ: the triangle was wrong. Its apex was drawn sharp at (52.5,35.5) at the top-left edge of the ink; the print has a blunt apex at about 51.7-55.6, y 37-38. The closing bar was about 2 units too low (now 50.2 to 48.3, sloping up to the right). The descender turns at about (64,58) and the base line lies at y 62.6-63, not 61.5. Redrawn from skeleton fits that agree in all three copies; strokes text updated.

Syriac #18 ṣād: the head was about 2 units too high and the turn-back point misplaced, so 2% of the trace was off the ink and 12% of the ink was missed. The head was lowered and the turn rerouted through (63.5,46) to (56,52.5). The trace is now fully on the ink, with 99% coverage.

findings: Method: I re-cut every cell from the Wellcome JP2 leaves (b22039910_0205 for Plato, b22039910_0175 for Jupiter). I overlaid each path on its cell and compared it with the ink skeleton, which showed off-ink path, missed strokes and offsets. I also checked every ring and dot for an enclosed opening, and confirmed each Arabic label and the row order (right to left) by reading the table.

Two more copies of the 1806 printing were used as witnesses, both 500 ppi Internet Archive scans with no rights field: the Getty copy (ancientalphabets01ibnw, page n206 for Arabic p. 18 and n176 for p. 48) and the UNC copy (ancientalphabets00ibnw, page n23 for p. 18 and n53 for p. 48). I registered each page onto the Wellcome leaf with SIFT plus a RANSAC similarity fit (scale 1.24 to 1.26, rotation under 0.5 degrees) and refined each cell by correlation (NCC 0.94 to 0.98). The cells of all three copies therefore share the glyph frame. The registered cells were working files and are not kept. URLs actually fetched: https://archive.org/metadata/ancientalphabets01ibnw, https://archive.org/metadata/ancientalphabets00ibnw, https://archive.org/metadata/ancientalphabet00hammgoog, https://archive.org/metadata/ancientalphabet00conggoog, https://archive.org/metadata/10219150bsb, https://archive.org/download/ancientalphabets01ibnw/ancientalphabets01ibnw_page_numbers.json, https://archive.org/download/ancientalphabets00ibnw/ancientalphabets00ibnw_page_numbers.json, and https://archive.org/download/ancientalphabets01ibnw/page/n{208,206,176}.jpg plus https://archive.org/download/ancientalphabets00ibnw/page/n{208,206,176,30,60,23,53}.jpg (all HTTP 200). Only n206/n176 (Getty) and n23/n53 (UNC) are recorded in glyphs.json. The Oxford/Google and BSB scans were not compared.

Plato (Arabic p. 18): the labels and order (ا…ط, ي…ص, ق ر ش ت) are correct, and all 22 signs have the same form in the three copies. The tracing was already tight: path centrelines are on average 0.4 to 0.8 units from the ink skeleton, and no path runs off the ink. The one real form error was ق (see corrections).

Jupiter (Arabic p. 48): the labels and order are correct, and 27 of the 28 signs agree across the three copies. ط does not: the Wellcome copy prints only the two bars with their rings and lacks the right-hand side. Both Getty and UNC print a closed ⊐, which is the left-right mirror of ي. Whether the Wellcome gap comes from inking or from damage cannot be told, and the note says so.

Every Jupiter ring centre agrees with the opening in the print to within about 1 unit in all three copies. Two round ends that are filled in the Wellcome copy show an opening at the same place in both Getty and UNC: the upper end of خ (Getty opening about 3.5 units across, 10.6 square units) and the lower right end of ف (about 3 units, 5 to 7 square units).

These points stay unresolved and are labelled that way, at medium confidence. The top-right end of Jupiter ز has a tiny opening in all three copies (1 to 3 square units); it is drawn as a ring. The lower-left end of Jupiter س has a pinhole of about 1 unit in Getty and UNC and none in the Wellcome copy; it is drawn as a ball. The dot between the legs of Plato س is printed in all three copies, so it belongs to the printing block, but whether it was meant as part of the letter cannot be told.
Plato ف: the short dash above the start of the hook is in the Wellcome copy only and absent from both Getty and UNC. It is a mark of that one copy and stays undrawn; ف is re-rated to high.

Small things checked and left alone: a speck of about 1 unit inside the right-hand angle of Plato ق appears in Getty and UNC only and is noted, not drawn. Stray marks near Jupiter م appear in the UNC copy only. The short downward tail under the V of Jupiter ش appears in all three copies and stays. The open loop of Plato ل and the single body hole of Plato ص were confirmed in all three copies.

Final runs: glyphkit/check.mjs gives 'ok: 22 letters, 0 gaps' (plato) and 'ok: 28 letters, 0 gaps' (jupiter). The overlays and specimen sheets were made again for both tables and read. The last overlay sweep found no path off the ink by more than 1 unit, the worst being Jupiter م at 1.0 unit on a stroke edge.
